article.excerpt: "Miss na miss kita" is not "miss" said twice for emphasis. It is Tagalog’s X na X intensive, and the na inside it is the linker — a different headword in the national dictionary from the na in "miss na kita". The construction is corpus-attested; this instance of it is not.

article.metaDescription: Miss na miss kita means "I miss you very much" — Tagalog’s X na X intensive. That na is the linker, not the "already" na: 2 separate KWF dictionary headwords.

keyTakeaways: "Miss na miss kita" means "I miss you very much", and the doubling is a Tagalog construction — X na X — not the English habit of repeating a word for emphasis.
The na inside it is the linker (pang-angkop), a separate headword in the KWF national dictionary from the na of "miss na kita", which is the adverb meaning "already; by now".
The linker rule is testable: it surfaces as -ng after a vowel, which is why the corpus has bagong-bago and masayang-masaya but pagod na pagod, mahal na mahal and miss na miss.

Tatoeba attests the frame with the same pronoun in "Mahal na mahal kita" = "I love you very much", but returned 0 sentences for "miss na miss kita" on 25 September 2026 — the construction is attested, this instance of it is not.
Across 214 miss-you pages on SubhSandesh, recipients tapped a hug button 1,434 times on 138 of them and 512 times on one page, while the median letter runs just 88 words.

faqs.question: Is "miss na miss kita" grammatically correct Tagalog?
faqs.answer: Nothing fetched for this page marks it wrong, and every piece of it is independently attested: the X na X frame, the linker allomorph after a consonant, and the pronoun kita in "Mahal na mahal kita" on Tatoeba. What is missing is a corpus sentence containing the whole phrase, which is a gap in the corpus rather than a verdict on the sentence.

faqs.question: What is the difference between "miss na kita" and "miss na miss kita"?
faqs.answer: Different words spelled the same. The na in "miss na kita" is the adverb the KWF dictionary files under pang-abay, meaning "already; by now" — the same particle as in tapos na. The na in "miss na miss kita" is the linker, pang-angkop, and it is doing degree rather than time.

faqs.question: Can you say "miss na miss na miss kita"?
faqs.answer: The construction takes a third copy in general: Tatoeba attests "Gutom na gutom na gutom na ako", translated "I am terribly hungry" against "very hungry" for the two-copy version. Whether anyone says it with miss is not something any source fetched here records, so treat the triple as playful rather than standard.

faqs.question: Why is it "pagod na pagod" but "bagong-bago"?
faqs.answer: Because of one rule in the KWF entry for the linker: na becomes ng when the preceding word ends in a vowel. Pagod ends in a consonant, so the linker stays na and the phrase is written as three words. Bago ends in a vowel, so the linker attaches as -ng and the pair is conventionally hyphenated.

faqs.question: Is "sobrang miss kita" better than doubling the word?
faqs.answer: It is the version with more corpus support for this particular verb. Tatoeba has "Sobrang miss ko na ang Boston" translated "I miss Boston so much", using the adverb sobrang instead of the doubled frame. Both mean roughly the same thing; sobrang sounds slightly more like writing and less like speech.

faqs.question: Does "namimiss na namimiss kita" work?
faqs.answer: It stacks the ongoing conjugated form inside the intensive, and nothing fetched here attests it. Tatoeba does carry "Namimiss ko na siya" and "Mamimiss din kita", so the conjugated forms themselves are real; the doubled version of them is not in the corpus and this page does not claim it is.

faqs.question: Is "miss na miss kita" the same kind of phrase as "mahal na mahal kita"?
faqs.answer: Structurally, yes — identical frame, identical pronoun, and Tatoeba sentence 11557704 translates "Mahal na mahal kita" as "I love you very much". The only difference is that mahal is a native Tagalog root and miss is an English loan, which is exactly what makes the borrowed version interesting.

faqs.question: Is it too intense to send to someone I have just started seeing?
faqs.answer: Probably, and that is the point of the construction rather than an accident of it. The intensive means saturation, so it reports a state you are already in. "Miss kita" or "miss na kita" says the same thing without the claim about degree.

faqs.question: How do I know whether the person speaks Tagalog or Cebuano?
faqs.answer: Ask, rather than guessing from the country. The doubling construction exists across Philippine languages but the words filling it do not transfer, and Cebuano handles missing someone with an entirely different root. Guessing wrong undoes the reason you reached for the language in the first place.

faqs.question: How long should the message around the line be?
faqs.answer: The median letter across 214 miss-you pages on SubhSandesh is 88 words and the longest is 1,024. An intensive costs one word; the remaining 87 are where a specific memory goes, and specificity is what the doubling cannot supply on its own.

faqs.question: Should I password-protect a page before sending it?
faqs.answer: 43.5% of miss-you senders do, against 38.5% of creators platform-wide, which makes it the most private segment measured on the platform. It only helps if the recipient opens it on their own device — on a shared phone a password is an obstacle rather than a protection.

faqs.question: Is a voice note better than writing it?
faqs.answer: For this phrase specifically, often yes. The intensive carries stress and vowel length that spelling does not reproduce, and 13.6% of miss-you senders record a voice note. If the doubling is the whole message, saying it aloud delivers more of it than typing it does.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Miss Na Miss Kita: What the Doubled Word Is Actually Doing

**Miss na miss kita** means "I miss you very much", and the doubling is where the "very" lives. But it is not the English habit of repeating a word for emphasis. It is a regular Tagalog construction — **X na X** — that copies a root around a linker to mean "X to the point of saturation", and the *na* holding the two halves together is a different word from the *na* in *miss na kita*. They are separate headwords in the national dictionary. This page pulls the two particles apart, tests the construction against an open corpus, and sets it beside 214 "I miss you" pages built on SubhSandesh since 28 July 2026, where recipients have tapped a hug button 1,434 times across 138 of those pages and the median letter runs 88 words.

## What each piece of "miss na miss kita" is doing

*Miss na miss kita* has four slots: the borrowed English verb *miss*, the linker *na*, a second copy of *miss*, and *kita*. The last one is the only piece that is purely Tagalog grammar — [English Wiktionary's entry](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/kita#Tagalog) defines *kita* as the pronoun that replaces *ko ka* or *ko ikaw*, fusing "I" and "you" into one word. That is settled ground — the [guide to "I miss you" in different languages](/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages) lists the Tagalog line among fifty others — and it is not what this page is about.

What is left — *miss na miss* — is the interesting part, because the intensifying frame is native and the thing sitting inside it is not.

## The two "na"s, and why nobody tells them apart

There is more than one Tagalog word spelled *na*, and the difference is the single most useful thing to take away from this page. The [KWF Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino](https://diksiyonaryo.ph/search/na), the national dictionary, gives them as **separate headwords**:

- ***na*, pnk** (*pang-angkop*, the linker): "nag-uugnay sa pang-uri at pangngalan" — it joins an adjective to a noun, as in *matinis na boses*, "a piercing voice". The entry adds the rule that decides everything below: it "becomes *ng* if the preceding word ends in a vowel".
- ***na*, pnb** (*pang-abay*, adverb): "nagpapahayag ng kaganapan kapag sumusunod sa isang pandiwa" — it marks the event as accomplished when it follows a verb, as in *tapos na*, "finished already".

[Wiktionary's Tagalog entry](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/na#Tagalog) separates them by ancestry too. The "already; now; anymore" adverb is inherited from Proto-Philippine **\*na* "now; already". The linker comes from a different reconstruction entirely, Proto-Austronesian **\*na*, glossed there as a "linker marking emphatic attribution" — emphasis built into the etymology.

So the three lines a searcher runs together are three different sentences:

- **Miss kita** — the flat statement, with nothing added.
- **Miss na kita** — the *adverb* na. "I miss you by now." Tatoeba's Tagalog corpus attests the same particle on the same borrowed verb in *Miss ko na si Tom*, translated "I already miss Tom".
- **Miss na miss kita** — the *linker* na, doing degree rather than time.

One Tatoeba sentence carries both at once: *Gutom na gutom na ako*, "I'm very hungry". The first *na* is the linker holding the intensive together; the second is the "already" adverb. Nothing on the results page for this phrase makes that distinction, and it is the whole grammar of the thing.

## How to prove X na X is a construction and not a habit

Four pieces of evidence, all checkable, none of them about *miss*.

### 1. It works on roots that have nothing to do with each other

Tatoeba's Tagalog corpus attests the frame across word classes with English glosses attached: [*pagod na pagod*](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/search?query=pagod+na+pagod&from=tgl) "very tired", *galit na galit* "furious", *takot na takot* "scared stiff", *gutom na gutom* "very hungry", *ayaw na ayaw* "I hate". A construction that takes any root and returns the same meaning shift is a rule, not an idiom.

### 2. The linker changes shape exactly as the dictionary says it should

The KWF entry says *na* becomes *ng* after a vowel. Test it: *pagod*, *galit*, *takot*, *gutom*, *mahal* all end in consonants and take *na*. *Bago* and *masaya* end in vowels — and the corpus gives *bagong-bago*, "brand new", and *masayang-masaya*, "very happy", with the linker suffixed as *-ng* and the pair written with a hyphen.

*Miss* ends in /s/. The construction therefore predicts *na*, and *miss na miss* is what people say. English repetition has no reason to insert a Tagalog linker between two copies, still less the correct allomorph of one.

### 3. It scales

The frame takes a third copy. Tatoeba attests *Gutom na gutom na gutom na ako*, glossed "I am terribly hungry" — one step up from the two-copy "very hungry". A fixed idiom cannot do that; a degree construction can.

### 4. The typology already records this device for Tagalog

Copying a whole word to shift its meaning is ordinary morphology. Carl Rubino's [WALS chapter on reduplication](https://wals.info/chapter/27) defines full reduplication as "the repetition of an entire word, word stem (root with one or more affixes), or root", and counts 278 of the 368 languages surveyed as using partial and full reduplication productively, with a further 35 using full reduplication only.

His worked Tagalog example is a meaning shift of exactly this shape: *mag-isip*, "to think", against *mag-isip-isip*, "to think about seriously". That example is word-internal and *miss na miss* is phrasal, with an independent linker sitting between the copies — but the move it makes, copy the root and get a stronger reading, is one the typology already files under this language.

## Is "miss na miss kita" actually attested?

Here the honest answer is more interesting than a confident one. Searched on 25 September 2026, Tatoeba's Tagalog corpus returns **zero** sentences for *miss na miss kita*, and zero for *miss kita* and *miss na kita* as well.

The construction is attested. This instance of it is not.

Two findings make that precise rather than damning. First, the identical frame with the identical pronoun is in the corpus: [*Mahal na mahal kita*](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/search?query=mahal+na+mahal+kita&from=tgl), translated "I love you very much". Frame, linker and *kita* are all corpus-verified — only the filler differs.

Second, where the corpus does intensify *miss*, it reaches for a different device: *Sobrang miss ko na ang Boston*, "I miss Boston so much", using *sobrang* rather than doubling.

Tatoeba is a volunteer corpus with thin Tagalog coverage, so absence there is weak evidence of anything. It is not evidence that the phrase is wrong. It is a reason to say "attested construction, unattested instance" instead of pretending to a citation that does not exist.

## The three lines side by side

| Line | Which *na* | What it adds | In Tatoeba (tgl), 25 Sep 2026 | Against 214 miss-you pages |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Miss kita | none | The bare statement | 0 sentences | Leaves all 88 median words for something specific |
| Miss na kita | adverb (*pang-abay*) | Elapsed time: "by now" | 0 exact; *Miss ko na si Tom* attests the particle | 28.0% of senders set a reunion date — the same "by now" |
| Miss na miss kita | linker (*pang-angkop*) | Degree: saturation | 0 exact; *Mahal na mahal kita* attests the frame | 1,434 hug taps across 138 of 214 pages, 512 on one |
| Sobrang miss kita | none | Degree, by adverb instead | *Sobrang miss ko na ang Boston* attested | The line people use when the doubling feels like too much |

## What the doubling cannot do

Saying it harder is not the same as saying it fully, and the first-party numbers are blunt about which one recipients respond to. Across the 214 pages built on the `/missyou-gf` template since it went live on 28 July 2026 — 4.1% of 5,221 pages across 44 collections — the median letter is **88 words** and the longest is 1,024. An intensive costs you one word; the other 87 are where the specifics go.

The recipient-side number is the one no translation page has: **1,434 hug taps across 138 of the 214 pages**, and 512 on a single page. That is the reader doing their own X na X — repeating a gesture until it means something. It is also the strongest argument for a format that accepts repetition, which a text message does not.

Three limits travel with every number here. The city, background-music and "together since" fields are **pickers with defaults**, so no fill rate on them is evidence of what a sender chose. `viewCount` counts page views and not unique visitors — the 2,417 recorded views, 11.3 per page and 104 on the most-opened one, may be a handful of people returning. And n = 214 over two months supports no seasonal claim at all.

If the line is going somewhere a text gets buried, the [miss-you page for a partner](/missyou-gf) is the format these numbers describe.

## When to send something other than this

If the person reads on a shared phone, a page is the wrong call and the 43.5% of miss-you senders who password-protect before sharing — against 38.5% of creators platform-wide, the most private segment measured here — are building a barrier rather than a protection. Send a voice note instead; 13.6% of senders record one, and *miss na miss kita* said aloud carries stress and length that no spelling reproduces.

If the problem is that the words themselves are not enough — which is, after all, why the language doubled one in the first place — [Hold My Hand](/hold-my-hand) suits this reader better than a letter does: the recipient holds the screen for sixty seconds without letting go, it drains if they release, and the letter unlocks only at the end. Saturation, as a thing you do rather than a thing you write. [Browse the other templates](/templates) if neither fits.

And if you are not sure the recipient speaks Tagalog rather than Cebuano, Ilocano or Bikol, ask before you send. The doubling exists in those languages too; the words around it do not.

## Sources

- English Wiktionary, *na* (Tagalog): https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/na#Tagalog
- KWF Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino, *na*: https://diksiyonaryo.ph/search/na
- Tatoeba, Tagalog X na X intensives: https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/search?query=pagod+na+pagod&from=tgl
- Tatoeba, *Mahal na mahal kita* and the *miss* queries: https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/search?query=mahal+na+mahal+kita&from=tgl
- Rubino, C., "Reduplication", in Dryer, M. S. & Haspelmath, M. (eds.), *WALS Online*, 2013, CC BY 4.0: https://wals.info/chapter/27

sources.stat: English Wiktionary lists three separate Tagalog etymologies for na. Etymology 2, inherited from Proto-Philippine *na "now; already", gives the adverb "already; now; anymore (expresses the event when following a verb)", example Tapos na, "Finished already". Etymology 3, inherited from Proto-Austronesian *na glossed "linker marking emphatic attribution", gives the ligature that "Connects adjectives to nouns" (May matinis na boses siya) and whose usage note states that "na becomes the -ng suffix if the preceding word ends in a vowel".

The KWF Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino carries na as separate headwords: na pnk (pang-angkop) "1: nag-uugnay sa pang-uri at pangngalan, hal matinis na boses; matangkad na lalaki 2: nag-uugnay sa pang-abay at pandiwa; nagiging ng kung nagtatapos sa patinig ang sinusundang salita"; and na pnb (pang-abay) "1: nagpapahayag ng kaganapan kapag sumusunod sa isang pandiwa, hal tapos na; yari na". A third headword na pnr covers Bagsak na / Ako na, and na- pnl is the verbal prefix.

Tatoeba Tagalog sentences attest the X na X frame across word classes with English translations: "Pagod na pagod nga sila." = "They were very tired indeed."; "Galit na galit ang mga republikano." = "Republicans were furious."; "Takot na takot ako." = "I was scared stiff."; "Gutom na gutom na ako." = "I’m very hungry."; "Ayaw na ayaw kong sumayaw." = "I hate dancing."; the vowel-final roots take the -ng allomorph, "Bagong-bago ang motor ni Tom." = "Tom’s motorcycle is brand new." and "Masayang-masaya si Tom." = "Tom is very happy."; and the frame iterates, "Gutom na gutom na gutom na ako." = "I am terribly hungry."

Tatoeba sentence #11557704, "Mahal na mahal kita.", is translated "I love you very much." / "I love you a lot." — the X na X frame with the pronoun kita. Searched from=tgl on 25 September 2026, the corpus returned 0 sentences containing "miss na miss kita", 0 containing "miss kita" and 0 containing "miss na kita"; it does attest "Miss ko na si Tom." = "I already miss Tom." and "Sobrang miss ko na ang Boston." = "I miss Boston so much."

Carl Rubino defines full reduplication as "the repetition of an entire word, word stem (root with one or more affixes), or root" and gives a Tagalog example of a meaning shift produced by it: mag-isip "to think" vs mag-isip-isip "to think about seriously". The accompanying Feature 27A counts 278 languages with productive full and partial reduplication, 35 with full reduplication only and 55 with no productive reduplication, out of 368 surveyed.

structuralLimitations: THE PROMPT’S CENTRAL CLAIM IS CONFIRMED, BUT ITS NAME FOR THE MECHANISM WAS INCOMPLETE. The task prompt framed the angle as "the na ... na REDUPLICATION". Verified on 2026-09-25: the doubling is real and productive, but the piece between the copies is not part of a reduplicative affix — it is the LINKER (pang-angkop), a separate word with its own headword in the KWF Diksiyonaryo ng Wikang Filipino ("na pnk: nag-uugnay sa pang-uri at pangngalan") and its own etymology on Wiktionary (Proto-Austronesian *na, "linker marking emphatic attribution"), distinct from the Proto-Philippine *na "now; already" that gives the adverb. Calling it reduplication without naming the linker misses the one piece of evidence that decides the case, which is the allomorphy: the KWF entry states na becomes ng after a vowel, and the corpus obeys it (bagong-bago, masayang-masaya vs pagod na pagod, mahal na mahal, galit na galit). The body therefore describes an X na X construction built on full-word copying plus the linker, and reserves "reduplication" for the affixal process the MEG paper studies.

THE CONSTRUCTION IS ATTESTED; THIS INSTANCE OF IT IS NOT. Searched on Tatoeba from=tgl on 2026-09-25 via the public api_v0 endpoint: "miss na miss kita" returned 0 sentences, "miss kita" 0, and "miss na kita" 0. The frame itself is attested with the same pronoun — sentence #11557704, "Mahal na mahal kita.", translated "I love you very much." The corpus also shows that where it does intensify the borrowed verb miss, it uses a different device: "Sobrang miss ko na ang Boston." = "I miss Boston so much." Tatoeba is a volunteer corpus with thin Tagalog coverage, so absence is weak evidence and the body says so explicitly rather than treating it as a verdict. The sibling post i-miss-you-in-tagalog cut "Miss na miss kita" as unattested; this post prints it as the keyword it was assigned and states the attestation gap in the body, which is the only honest way to write a page about a phrase that is everywhere on social media and nowhere in a corpus.

LINES CUT, WITH REASONS. Six. (1) The Aegis song "Miss na Miss Kita" — the SERP surfaced it via lyricstranslate, but the English Wikipedia API returned MISSING for that title on 2026-09-25, so no entity page verifies it exists under that name and every mention of it is cut. (2) "Miss na miss na miss kita" — not printed as a recommended line; the tripling is attested only for gutom ("Gutom na gutom na gutom na ako." = "I am terribly hungry."), so the body claims iteration for the construction and the FAQ says plainly that no source records it with miss. (3) "Namimiss na namimiss kita" — circulates widely, nothing fetched attests it; confined to an FAQ that says exactly that. (4) "Gandang-ganda" — the expected vowel-final example, but Tatoeba returned 0 exact matches for both gandang-ganda and "ganda na ganda" (the 5 hits were all ligature uses such as "Ang ganda ng karpet na ito"), so bagong-bago and masayang-masaya were used instead, both with 4 exact corpus hits. (5) "Sabik na sabik" — 4 fuzzy hits, 0 exact, so the native-root intensive named in the sibling’s territory is not printed here. (6) "Init na init" — 23 fuzzy hits, 0 exact; cut.

THE SCHOLARLY SOURCE WAS SWAPPED BECAUSE OF THE DOMAIN CAP, AND capcheck.mjs DOES NOT IMPLEMENT THE BRIEF’S RULE. The first choice was Wray, Stockall & Marantz, "Early Form-Based Morphological Decomposition in Tagalog: MEG Evidence from Reduplication, Infixation, and Circumfixation" (Neurobiology of Language 3(2):235–255, 16 February 2022, CC BY 4.0), whose full text was read at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10158618/ after direct.mit.edu and doi.org/10.1162/nol_a_00062 both returned HTTP 403 behind Cloudflare on 2026-09-25. It was CUT. The BRIEF §4 states that europepmc.org and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov "are the same domain for this purpose"; counted that way, i-miss-you-in-japanese, i-miss-you-in-spanish and say-i-miss-you-without-saying-it already hold three posts on it, so this post would have been the fourth and over cap. capcheck.mjs counts the two hosts SEPARATELY and reported no breach — it does not implement the BRIEF’s equivalence rule, and a later agent trusting its output alone will breach this cap without being told. doi.org was also avoided (it stood at 2 posts, and the sibling i-miss-you-in-tagalog already notes it resolves to linguisticsociety.org). The replacement is Rubino’s WALS chapter on a fresh domain. THE REPLACEMENT DOES NOT STUDY THIS CONSTRUCTION EITHER: Rubino describes word-internal full reduplication and his Tagalog example (mag-isip vs mag-isip-isip) has no linker standing between the copies. He is cited for the definition, the 278/35/55-of-368 typological counts and that one Tagalog example, and the body states the word-internal versus phrasal difference in the same paragraph rather than letting the citation carry more than it says.

CANNIBALISATION: THREE PHILIPPINE SIBLINGS IN ONE BATCH, DIVIDED BY MECHANISM NOT LANGUAGE. i-miss-you-in-tagalog owns the lexical and aspectual question — kita as the ko ka portmanteau, the ma-/na- loan-verb paradigm, pangungulila and sabik, and the KWF miss entry with its six "mabigong" senses. no-tagalog-word-for-miss owns the borrowability question — why verbs are borrowed less readily than nouns, with the World Loanword Database. miss-kita-in-bisaya owns Cebuano. THIS post owns exactly one thing neither of them touches: the two na particles and the X na X intensive. Checked directly on 2026-09-25: no-tagalog-word-for-miss contains no instance of "na miss", "redupl", "linker" or "pang-angkop" anywhere in its body, and i-miss-you-in-tagalog treats na only as the "already" adverb in one H3 and explicitly cut "Miss na miss kita". The Tagalog sibling’s KWF finding is cited here in a single clause and not retold. Against live content: Strapi returned 0 articles whose slug contains "kita", "tagalog", "filipino" or "na-miss" on 2026-09-25. The live hub /blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages was fetched the same day (1,276 words in contentMarkdown) and contains the string "miss na miss" zero times and "redupl" zero times — its only Philippine content is the list line "Tagalog (Filipino): Miss na kita / Nami-miss kita" and one table row. This post links up to the hub and restates nothing from it.

SERP: ONE SEARCH, US-SERVED, NO COMPETITOR CLAIM MADE. One WebSearch on the exact keyword "miss na miss kita meaning" was run on 2026-09-25 and returned forum.wordreference.com, lyricstranslate.com, italki.com, learnwitholiver.com, wordhippo.com, en.wikipedia.org (Miss Kita Kung Christmas — off-intent), mymemory.translated.net, spanishdict.com (wrong language entirely), hinative.com and brainly.ph. This is a US-served SERP; no India-served or Philippines-served SERP was run, and the body makes no claim about what any of these pages rank for or contain beyond the search engine’s own summary, which asserted that "the word is repeated to put more stress on it, and in Tagalog, this word repetition is used instead of words like very or so". That summary is correct as far as it goes and stops exactly where this post starts: it names no particle, no linker, no allomorphy and no attestation.

THE ORTHOGRAPHY IS UNSETTLED AND NO SOURCE SETTLES IT. The corpus writes the consonant-final intensives as three separate words (pagod na pagod) and the vowel-final ones with a hyphen (bagong-bago, masayang-masaya). Nothing fetched states a spelling rule for the hyphen, and English Wiktionary returned HTTP 404 for the lemmas "pagod na pagod", "mahal na mahal", "gutom na gutom", "ayaw na ayaw", "miss na miss" and "bagong-bago" alike, so none of these phrases is lemmatised there. The body reports the pattern as observed convention rather than as a rule.

REGISTER, FREQUENCY AND REGION ARE UNMEASURED. Nothing fetched measures how often "miss na miss kita" is used, by whom, in which region, or against which alternative. The body orders the three lines by what the grammar adds, not by frequency, and makes no frequency claim anywhere. No usage statistic for any Philippine language appears in this post.

FIRST-PARTY SEGMENT IS SUBHSANDESH’S AND IS NOT FILIPINO-SPECIFIC. The 214 miss-you pages are drawn from an Indian-audience platform with a 15-city picker; nothing in the segment identifies a sender or recipient as a Tagalog speaker. The numbers describe how a miss-you page behaves, not how Filipino senders behave, and the body does not claim otherwise. The three mandatory caveats — pickers with defaults, viewCount as page views rather than unique visitors, and n = 214 over two months from 2026-07-28 supporting no seasonal claim — all appear in body prose in the section where the numbers are used.

TEMPLATE COLLISION WITH A CONCURRENT SIBLING, DECIDED ON MERIT. /hold-my-hand was chosen as the oneOfLinks alternative before no-tagalog-word-for-miss.json appeared in the batch directory, and that sibling has taken the same link. It is kept here rather than swapped for novelty, because the reason is specific to this post: the X na X intensive means saturation, and Hold My Hand is the only template in oneOfLinks whose mechanic is sustained unbroken contact that drains when released. /streak was the considered alternative and was rejected because it models iteration across days rather than saturation in one utterance.

SOURCE CAPS AT TIME OF WRITING. capcheck.mjs was re-run immediately before saving. diksiyonaryo.ph is used here as its third post in the batch (after i-miss-you-in-tagalog and no-tagalog-word-for-miss), which is AT the domain cap of 3 and not over it; the URL /search/na is new to the batch and the two URLs already at the 2-post URL cap (/search/miss and /search/pangungulila) are not used. A later agent must not cite diksiyonaryo.ph at all. wals.info was unused in the batch before this post. europepmc.org / pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and doi.org were deliberately avoided; see the source-swap note above. tatoeba.org and en.wiktionary.org are in capExemptDomains and were still fetched and read rather than quoted from memory.

failed.item: Every H2 section answerable standalone in 2–3 sentences
failed.why: "How to prove X na X is a construction and not a habit" is four independent tests — root-generality, the linker allomorph, iteration to a third copy, and the typological record for Tagalog. A 2–3 sentence standalone answer has to drop two of the four, and each test is load-bearing because the post’s whole claim is that the doubling is morphology rather than emphasis. Structural: closes only if the four tests are split across separate H2s, which would break the argument into pieces that no longer read as a proof.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on this SERP that separates the two Tagalog na particles by dictionary headword and by etymology, and the only one that tests the X na X intensive with the linker allomorphy rule (bagong-bago vs pagod na pagod) and with the corpus result that the frame is attested with kita in "Mahal na mahal kita" while the exact phrase returns zero hits — the competing pages assert "repeat the word for emphasis" and stop. Against that: SubhSandesh has no authority in Philippine linguistics, the phrase carries a song title and heavy social-media usage that will keep entertainment and forum results above it for a long time, and the realistic upside is being cited by an answer engine asked which na is which, not a Google position.
